judgment.thesis: Credo has proprietary SerDes/DSP IP and a Microsoft-partnered AEC product, and revenue is growing 224% with operating margin swinging from -15% to +25%, so this looks like a real AI-connectivity share gainer rather than a price-driven recovery. It is not a clear diamond: customer concentration is likely high, competition from Broadcom, Marvell and optical alternatives is strong, and the filings supplied give no backlog, contract or named-customer figures to confirm the demand.
judgment.breaks_if: A top hyperscaler customer cuts or dual-sources AEC orders, sequential revenue growth stalls, or gross margin falls below about 60% as larger competitors price aggressively.
judgment.customers: Hyperscalers and cloud providers (all major ones engaged), plus OEMs, ODMs, optical module makers, MSOs and MNOs; Microsoft is the only named partner; concentration is not quantified in the supplied text but is likely high.
red_flags: Backlog and deferred revenue not reported, so forward demand cannot be verified
Customer concentration not quantified; likely a few hyperscalers drive most revenue
Edge claims (n-1 advantage, best-in-class) are management's own words, not evidence of lock-in
IP license revenue fell from 15% to 3% of sales; growth is mostly lumpy hardware sales
Insiders (CEO, CFO, CTO) have 10b5-1 plans to sell shares; share count up 5%

judgment.thesis: Gulfport is a natural gas-weighted E&P selling a commodity, so its swing from a -25% to a +42% operating margin most likely reflects gas prices and the post-bankruptcy cost base rather than any durable advantage. It is not a diamond: nothing in the evidence shows pricing power, customer dependence or contracted demand, and the production outlook is only roughly flat to modestly up.
judgment.breaks_if: Henry Hub and Appalachian gas prices fall back and the operating margin compresses toward zero; equally, evidence of long-term fixed-price or take-or-pay contracts with named buyers would be needed to change this view.
judgment.customers: not disclosed (sells natural gas, NGLs and oil at market-linked prices; buyer concentration not given in the excerpts)
red_flags: Commodity producer: the margin swing tracks gas prices, with no evidence of an edge
Revenue growth of +48% to +147% looks price-driven, plus the 2020 Chapter 11 reset of the cost base
2026 guidance of 1.030-1.055 Bcfe/d implies modest volume growth, not an inflection
No backlog, prepaid revenue, named customers or contract data disclosed
Capital returned through buybacks (about $336M in 2025) at about $189/share while relying on revolver borrowings, and 8% notes due May 2026

judgment.thesis: BRUKINSA is a real product advantage: the broadest BTK label in the class, head-to-head superiority over ibrutinib, $3.9B in 2025 sales and global market leadership. Sonrotoclax approval and a degrader pipeline could extend the franchise, so the profit inflection looks operating-leverage-driven rather than a recovery from a collapse. But the evidence is thin on contracts or backlog, the market is crowded with strong rivals, and the $449B market value (as supplied) looks very large against $5.3B
judgment.breaks_if: BRUKINSA growth slows sharply or its US share falls to acalabrutinib or pirtobrutinib, or the FDA delays or rejects sonrotoclax in 1H 2026, so operating margin stalls near zero while R&D and SG&A stay high.
judgment.customers: Not disclosed in the excerpts; sales are to hospitals, specialty pharmacies and distributors across the US, Europe, China and 75+ markets, with likely wholesaler concentration and exposure to government payers and China pricing.
red_flags: Operating margin only 8%; the 9-month figure is $262M on $3.8B revenue, still thin
Third entrant in a crowded BTK/BCL2 market against AbbVie, J&J, AstraZeneca and Lilly
Net income of $287M and positive FCF are helped by an $885M sale of future royalties and heavy stock compensation ($387M over 9 months)
No backlog or deferred revenue disclosed, so demand rests on prescription trends the excerpts do not show
IRA pricing pressure, China exposure, and a share count up 4% from dilution

judgment.thesis: Matrix-M adjuvant is a real proprietary asset, validated by Sanofi's non-exclusive license, the Pfizer license (January 2026) and the R21 malaria vaccine. But the profit swing looks like recognition of previously deferred APA revenue and cost cuts from a restructuring, not durable demand, and the core COVID product faces shrinking, policy-exposed demand. This reads as a recovery from collapse, not an inflection.
judgment.breaks_if: Revenue stays dependent on recognizing deferred APA balances, Australia or Gavi cancel or demand refunds, and Matrix-M licensing (Pfizer, Sanofi, material transfer agreements) produces no milestone or royalty revenue to replace COVID sales.
judgment.customers: Governments and agencies via advance purchase agreements (Australia, Gavi, others), plus Sanofi, Pfizer and Serum Institute as partners; concentration is high but exact shares are not given.
red_flags: Deferred revenue fell 56% on the year, so the revenue and margin jump likely reflects earlier prepayments being recognized, not new orders
Going-concern language appears in the 10-Q, and a restructuring plan is in place
Australia APA: doses cancelled, TGA application withdrawn, up to $92.5M of deferred revenue possibly refundable
Heavy dependence on Serum Institute for co-formulation and filling, and on a single COVID product amid vaccine policy and reimbursement risk
Matrix-M deals are non-exclusive and early-stage, with no disclosed economics; backlog not reported; share count up 6%

judgment.thesis: Marvell has real technical positions in custom AI ASICs and optical DSPs, and data center revenue rose to 72% of sales (from 40%) in FY2025. But the evidence supplied names no customers, backlog or contracts, and the headline profit turn is flattered by a one-off $1.83B gain on sale of a business and by a recovery from a restructuring-hit year, so it is not clearly different.
judgment.breaks_if: Data center revenue growth stalls or a top custom-ASIC customer moves its design in-house or to a rival such as Broadcom, leaving operating margin near 15% and gross margin falling back below 50%.

judgment.thesis: iRhythm has a real niche position in ambulatory cardiac monitoring (Zio), with FDA 510(k) clearances, a 71% gross margin and steady 26-27% growth. Operating margin has improved from -20% to -8%, but that improvement is partly because a $32M in-process R&D charge fell out of the comparison. The evidence supplied shows no named customer wins, backlog or signed contracts, so this reads as a good growth company still losing money rather than a clear inflection.
judgment.breaks_if: Revenue growth falls below about 20%, or gross margin stops rising, or Medicare/commercial payor reimbursement cuts hit the Zio services, or operating margin fails to reach breakeven over the next few quarters.
judgment.customers: Healthcare providers (cardiologists, primary care) order the service; revenue is paid mainly by Medicare and commercial payors. Concentration is not disclosed in the excerpts.

Highly competitive remote cardiac monitoring market, and 510(k) clearance is a lower barrier than PMA

judgment.thesis: Cerence has real incumbency: about 52% of new cars shipped carry its software, it has 25 years of OEM relationships, and it integrates deeply into vehicle programs. But the profit swing looks like a lumpy license recognition on top of a collapsed base, since FY25 revenue fell 24%, and OEMs and big-tech assistants could replace it. This looks more like a recovery from a trough than a clean inflection.
judgment.breaks_if: License revenue falls back toward the roughly $20-25M per quarter run-rate of the prior-year quarter, or the next two quarters show no sustained operating profit, which would mean the $87.8M license quarter was a one-off.
judgment.customers: Nearly all major automakers (BMW, Mercedes, VW Group, Stellantis, Toyota, Ford, GM, BYD and others) and tier-1 suppliers (Bosch, Continental, Harman, Aptiv). Over 80 OEMs and tier-1s use it. No single-customer percentage is given in the excerpts.
red_flags: Quarterly license revenue rose from $22.7M to $87.8M while connected and professional services were flat or down, which points to a lumpy upfront license recogn
FY25 revenue fell 24% and the prior-year loss was $588M, so this is a recovery from a collapse

OEMs building in-house or using big-tech AI assistants threatens the moat, and the share count is up 5%

judgment.thesis: Freshworks is a real, scaling SaaS business with 85% gross margin, a swing to a 2% operating margin, and backlog (+23%) and deferred revenue (+19%) growing faster than revenue, but it sells SMB and mid-market ITSM and CX tools in crowded markets against ServiceNow, Zendesk, Atlassian and Salesforce. Margin improvement comes mainly from cost cuts (R&D and sales spend flat or down), growth is decelerating (18% to 14% quarterly), and no named wins or dominant niche appear, so it is more a decent bu

judgment.customers: About 75,000 companies in roughly 170 countries; over 60% of ARR from customers with more than 250 employees; no single-customer concentration disclosed.

Operating margin gain driven by cost cuts (R&D down about 13% y/y in the quarter), not by operating leverage on accelerating revenue
Competes with larger rivals (ServiceNow, Zendesk, Salesforce, Atlassian); no evidence of high switching costs or dominant niche share
Cash and securities fell from about $1.07B to $813M in nine months, probably from buybacks or tax settlement on equity awards; stock compensation remains heavy
No named customer wins, contract values or net retention figures in the supplied text; AI offerings are unquantified

judgment.thesis: Silicon Labs is a credible IoT wireless chip supplier with real design-in stickiness and a 56% gross margin. But the recent growth looks like a recovery from an inventory-driven collapse, and the operating margin is still -13%. The pending $231/share all-cash acquisition by Texas Instruments caps the upside, so the stock is a merger-arbitrage situation, not an inflecting diamond.
judgment.breaks_if: The TI merger closes or is terminated, and the next quarters show revenue growth fading while operating margin stays negative, which would confirm the rebound was inventory restocking and not new demand.
judgment.customers: not disclosed; sells to IoT device makers across home, industrial, commercial and health markets, with no named customers or concentration data in the supplied text
red_flags: Pending all-cash $231/share takeover by Texas Instruments caps the upside; the price reflects the deal, not the fundamentals

No backlog, prepaid revenue, or named customer wins disclosed; deferred revenue is only $8M
Stock-based compensation of about $60M over nine months, and the share count is rising

judgment.thesis: Adtran is a broad telecom equipment supplier with 17-20% growth and a sharp margin recovery from -46% to -1%, but the evidence shows no proprietary lock-in and no named customer wins, so this looks like a cyclical recovery in a competitive market (fiber access, optical transport) rather than a diamond. The +66% jump in deferred revenue is the one real positive signal, but without backlog, named contracts, or an explanation it could just be timing, and the company just raised $201M in convertible

judgment.thesis: Aurinia's profit inflection is mostly cost-driven (SG&A fell from $42M to $26M a quarter) on a single approved drug, LUPKYNIS, which is growing 20-29% with an 88% gross margin and buybacks. It is a decent but not a diamond: one product faces newer lupus nephritis rivals, has a finite patent life, and has no clear signs of accelerating demand beyond what is already in the numbers.
judgment.breaks_if: LUPKYNIS net product sales growth falls below about 10% as competing lupus nephritis therapies (Benlysta, Gazyva) take share, or the aritinercept pipeline fails to replace the drug's eventual loss of exclusivity.

No backlog, named contract wins or prescription-count data in the evidence
Sales go through three distributors, so the buyers are concentrated

judgment.thesis: Tutor Perini is a long-established heavy civil and building contractor with real pre-qualification and bonding barriers on mega-projects, but it still wins largely through competitive bidding with thin margins and a history of project write-downs. The swing from a $107M operating loss to a $40M profit in Q3 is largely recovery from prior-year unfavorable adjustments, so this looks like a normalizing contractor rather than a hidden diamond.
judgment.breaks_if: Further negative estimate revisions, change-order disputes or cost overruns on the large mass-transit and Newark/Midtown projects push operating margin back to zero or below, or backlog stops growing.
judgment.customers: Public agencies (transit authorities, state and local governments, federal/military) and private developers; large individual projects likely concentrated, but specific percentages are not disclosed in the supplied text.
red_flags: Backlog figure not reported in the supplied data, so demand cannot be verified directly
Profit improvement partly due to absence of prior-year losses and $28M favorable settlement adjustments in Q2
History of project losses, claims and disputes that tie up working capital
Competitive-bid civil work where price is the main factor; construction margins are thin
Prepaid/deferred revenue up 51% is a modest positive but not a named contract win; federal awards flat ( $300M vs $312M)

judgment.thesis: Harrow is a real growth story: revenue is up 33-36%, gross margin is 75%, and VEVYE and IHEEZO are branded FDA-approved products. But the profit turn is thin, since net income is still negative year to date and leverage is heavy. Much of the portfolio is old, generic-exposed ophthalmic eye drops and cash-pay compounding that faces ordinary competition and regulatory risk, so this reads as a decent specialty pharma, not a hard-to-replace diamond.
judgment.breaks_if: Quarterly revenue growth falls well below 30% as VEVYE faces competing dry-eye drugs and compounding rules tighten, or operating income stays at or below roughly $15M a year while interest expense of about $25M a year keeps net income negative.
judgment.customers: More than 10,000 US eyecare prescribers and institutions; ImprimisRx is mostly cash-pay. Branded products are likely sold through wholesalers, but concentration is not disclosed in the supplied text.
red_flags: Net loss of $11.8M over nine months; Q3 net income of $1.0M came only after a $7.75M debt extinguishment loss
Heavy debt: $243M of notes at 8.6-11.9% coupons, with equity only $47M and interest expense about $19M over nine months
Compounding business sits in an FDA 503A/503B regulatory gray zone and prices below branded drugs

The +1691% deferred revenue change is from a base of $44K to $345K, which is immaterial and not a demand signal

judgment.thesis: Incyte has real regulatory and orphan-drug protection around Jakafi in rare blood cancers, with a 29% operating margin and 6% share shrink, and newer products (Opzelura, Niktimvo, Monjuvi in follicular lymphoma) are adding growth. But about 2028 Jakafi patent expiry and heavy dependence on a single drug make this a durable cash cow facing a cliff, not a clear diamond.
judgment.breaks_if: Jakafi US sales decline, or generic ruxolitinib enters before or around the 2028 patent expiry without Opzelura, Niktimvo, Monjuvi and Zynyz revenue replacing it.

Operating margin jump from 1% to 29% may reflect a prior-year one-off charge, not operating leverage
Pricing and reimbursement risk from government and insurers; IRA small-biotech exception is temporary

judgment.thesis: Samsara looks like a real diamond candidate: a 29-31% grower with 77% gross margin, an operating margin improving from -25% to -5%, and a system-of-record platform (video safety, telematics, equipment monitoring) that is sticky once installed across a fleet. The skepticism is that at $16.6B the market already prices in the inflection, and the evidence supplied shows scale and growth but not proof of unusually hard-to-replace technology, since competitors such as Motive, Geotab and Verizon Connec

Prepaid/deferred revenue growth of 18% lags revenue growth of 29%
Competitive telematics and video-safety market with several credible rivals; no federal awards or named-contract evidence in the supplied data

judgment.thesis: TheRealReal is the largest online authenticated luxury resale marketplace, with real network effects (over 80% of GMV from repeat consignors, 1M+ active buyers) and revenue growth accelerating to 18% in the latest quarter, but it still posts an operating loss and carries a heavy debt load. The edge is a service and trust moat rather than technology or regulatory protection, since supply is non-exclusive and competitors include Vestiaire, Fashionphile, eBay, and luxury brands' own resale programs
judgment.breaks_if: Quarterly revenue growth falls back below 10% or operating margin stops improving (e.g. stays negative through 2026), or consignor supply or take rate weakens, leaving the convertible and non-convertible debt to be refinanced from a thin cash balance.

Share count up 6% in a year, so existing holders are being diluted
Gross margin flat at 75%, so improvement comes from cost leverage, not pricing power; competition is broad and supply is non-exclusive

judgment.thesis: nLIGHT has proprietary vertically integrated high-power fiber and semiconductor laser technology and a growing defense directed-energy business, with federal awards up from $109M to $152M and latest-quarter growth of 71%. But it is still loss-making, its industrial and microfabrication lines are cyclical and price-eroding, and the filings show no backlog, named customer wins or signed contracts, so it is not yet clearly a diamond.

But the growth is steady rather than accelerating, much of the 'inflection' is already in the numbers, and nothing shows a new step-up in demand, so it looks like a decent compounder, not a hidden diamond.
judgment.breaks_if: Revenue growth falls below mid-teens, or backlog and deferred revenue growth falls behind revenue growth, while operating margin stays negative; this would show the sustainability/CSRD tailwind fading and the AI features failing to drive expansion.

judgment.thesis: DraftKings is a scaled leader in US online sports betting and iGaming with real regulatory licences and a known brand. But it competes with FanDuel, MGM, Caesars and now prediction markets on largely undifferentiated products, and its margin gains come from hold and promotional efficiency rather than a hard-to-replace product. The loss-to-profit turn is thin (operating margin about 0%), and it is an operating-leverage story in a competitive, tax-exposed industry rather than a hidden diamond.

judgment.thesis: Guidewire is the entrenched core-systems platform for P&C insurers, where policy, claims and billing run on its software under 5-7 year subscriptions priced on premium volume. That means high switching costs and a visible demand signal: revenue growth accelerating to 27%, backlog up 60%, and operating margin turning positive at 5% as the cloud transition scales. It is a quality compounder rather than a hidden diamond, and the turn to profit is early and thin.
